newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's beleaguered PM poised for budget battle.
newsitem.headline: Russia's beleaguered PM poised for budget battle.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin prepared to join battle with his parliamentary foes on Friday over his handling of the economy but the powerful Communist Party threatened to block the government's budget.
Leaving nothing to chance, Chernomyrdin ordered all his ministers to attend the session of the State Duma lower house to help defend the revised 1997 draft spending plans.
The prime minister also planned to deliver a report to deputies on his government's medium-term economic strategy.

Faced with strikes, slumping output and arduous talks with international lenders, Chernomyrdin has come under heavy fire from both the opposition-dominated Duma and the normally compliant upper chamber Federation Council.
The Council, composed of regional leaders, has called a special sitting on December 10 to review Chernomyrdin's record.

With President Boris Yeltsin still convalescing after heart surgery, the technocrat premier -- appointed to the job four years ago this month -- has been taking much of the blame as well as the responsibility for Russia's many problems.

"The situation in the economy is very complicated, especially the payment of wages and pensions," Chernomyrdin said on Thursday, referring to delayed payments that brought hundreds of thousands of miners out on indefinite strike this week.
In Russia's biggest coalmining region, the Kuzbass in Siberia, the strike appeared to be losing momentum on Thursday.
But Interfax news agency said the number of mines on strike nationwide had increased to 132 and quoted union leaders as saying the government's concessions so far were unacceptable.
The government blames the delays in wage payments on tax-dodging, a national pastime that has also held up sorely needed loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
At its Friday session the Duma, which rejected the cabinet's original draft budget, is to discuss a compromise spending plan prepared by a government-parliamentary arbitration commission.
On Thursday Chernomyrdin held talks with leaders of parliamentary factions, including communist chief Gennady Zyuganov and ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky.

Zyuganov said his party would not accept the revised budget as it stood. The communists argue that it does not adequately meet the needs of millions of Russians who have lost out under painful market reforms.
"We've said it before and I said it today, we will not support this budget," Zyuganov told reporters.

Zyuganov said he did not rule out that Chernomyrdin could make changes before the session that would appease the communists, including sacking some ministers. "Everything depends on what we are presented with," Zyuganov said.
The overworked premier could draw comfort from signs that Yeltsin, 65, was beginning to take on a more active role exactly one month after undergoing open heart surgery.
Yeltsin talked with U.S. President Bill Clinton by telephone and the two leaders agreed to meet next March, probably in the United States.
A Kremlin source told Interfax news agency Yeltsin would soon go on a series of trips around Russia and abroad.
Interfax quoted the source as saying: "A fair number of pressing matters have built up, which demand the personal presence of Boris Yeltsin to settle them."
He also reiterated the prognosis of presidential doctors that Yeltsin would be back at his desk in the Kremlin in the last 10 days of December.
